summary.text: A Bose–Einstein condensate is a state of matter typically formed when a gas of bosons at very low densities is cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero.
In it, a large fraction of the bosons occupy the lowest quantum state, so quantum effects such as wavefunction interference become apparent macroscopically.
Einstein predicted it in 1924 to 1925, building on a paper by Satyendra Nath Bose, and Cornell and Wieman created one in 1995 using rubidium atoms.

items.prompt: Why can a cloud of bosonic atoms pile into the same lowest state when cooled?

options.label: Bosons are allowed to occupy one quantum state together
Bosons attract each other with a force that grows with cold
Cold removes all their energy and stops them completely
Bosons turn into photons at low temperatures

items.explain: Bosons are allowed to share a quantum state, so cooling them lets them fall into the lowest accessible one.

items.prompt: Why can light, not just atoms, form this kind of state?

options.label: Photons are fermions that pair up at low temperatures
Photons are heavier than atoms, so they settle at rest
Light cannot form it, only atoms can
Photons are bosons, and photon condensates can be made in dye microcavities

items.explain: Bosons include the photon, and BECs of photons can be made in dye microcavities with wavelength-scale mirror separation.

items.prompt: Helium-3 is a fermion, yet it enters a superfluid phase. What explains this?

options.label: It turns into helium-4 as it is cooled
Pairs of its atoms form bosonic Cooper pairs, at a much lower temperature
Fermions become bosons once they are cold enough
Its atoms pair at higher temperatures than helium-4's

items.explain: Helium-3, a fermion, enters a superfluid phase at a much lower temperature, explained by the formation of bosonic Cooper pairs of two atoms.

items.prompt: Atomic hydrogen was pursued from 1976 but condensed only in 1998, after alkali gases. What gave alkali gases an edge?

options.label: They are much lighter atoms than hydrogen is
They are bosons while hydrogen atoms are not
They could be pre-cooled by laser cooling, a head start
They need no final cooling step at all

items.explain: Condensing alkali gases is easier because laser cooling can pre-cool them, unlike atomic hydrogen at the time.

items.prompt: Why must the original BEC theory be heavily modified for superfluid helium-4?

options.label: It is a liquid, so the atoms' interactions are relatively strong
It is too hot to be a condensate
It is a fermion, unlike the atoms in a gas
It has no atoms in the lowest state

items.explain: Superfluid helium-4 is a liquid rather than a gas, so interactions between the atoms are relatively strong, though condensation remains fundamental to its superfluidity.

items.prompt: A condensate is warmed well above its critical temperature. What happens to the share of atoms in the lowest state?

options.label: It rises to almost all of them
It falls to about none
It stays exactly the same
It doubles

items.explain: If the temperature is far above the critical temperature, the fraction in the lowest state is approximately zero.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A Bose–Einstein condensate, or BEC, is a state of matter usually made by chilling a very thin gas of bosons to very nearly absolute zero, which is 0 K or −273.15 °C. Bosons are particles that are allowed to share the same quantum state. In this deep cold, a large share of them settle together into the lowest quantum state. Quantum effects that normally stay at microscopic scale, especially wavefunction interference, then become visible at a large scale.

paragraphs.heading: A prediction from the 1920s
paragraphs.text: The idea dates to 1924–1925. Satyendra Nath Bose sent Einstein a paper on the statistics of light quanta, which are now called photons. Einstein was impressed, translated it into German himself and got it published in 1924. He then carried Bose's ideas over to matter, giving the concept of a Bose gas made of identical particles with whole-number spin. Einstein proposed that cooling such atoms far enough would make them drop, or condense, into the lowest quantum state open to them, forming a new kind of matter.

paragraphs.heading: The long chase in the lab
paragraphs.text: Making one took decades. A 1976 paper proposed using spin-polarized atomic hydrogen, and four separate research groups took up the idea right away. Cooling hydrogen proved technically hard, and it was not condensed until 1998. Alkali gases turned out to be easier, because laser cooling could chill them in advance, giving a head start before a final stage of forced evaporative cooling.

paragraphs.heading: Success in 1995
paragraphs.text: On 5 June 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman at the NIST–JILA lab in Boulder, Colorado made the first gaseous condensate. They cooled about two thousand rubidium-87 atoms to below 170 nanokelvins, using laser cooling plus magnetic evaporative cooling. Roughly four months later, a separate team led by Wolfgang Ketterle at MIT condensed sodium-23 with a hundred times more atoms. That let them observe two separate condensates interfering with each other. Cornell, Wieman and Ketterle shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics.

paragraphs.heading: A link to superfluids
paragraphs.text: Condensation also helps explain a strange liquid. In 1938, researchers found that helium-4 becomes a superfluid below 2.17 K. A superfluid has zero viscosity, meaning it can flow without losing energy, and quantized vortices exist in it. Its superfluidity was soon believed to come from partial Bose–Einstein condensation of the liquid, and condensation is still seen as basic to how helium-4 behaves as a superfluid.

paragraphs.heading: A growing field
paragraphs.text: Those early experiments founded the field of ultracold atoms. Today hundreds of research groups around the world make condensates of thin atomic vapours as a matter of routine. Many other kinds of atoms have been condensed since 1995, and BECs have also been made from molecules, polaritons and other quasi-particles.
